intro: Martha Argerich plays Prokofiev’s Toccata, which starts by passing a single D between the hands and ends by hurling it across the keyboard. Between those extremes, chromatic lines keep slipping beneath the repeated notes.

sections.label: A · One D between two hands
sections.mNote: Repeated notes widen into chromatic lines

sections.label: A′ · The repeated note returns quietly
sections.mNote: The opening figure returns before the hands pull apart

sections.label: Dev · Triads against chromatic lines
sections.mNote: The hands descend at different times, then climb apart

sections.label: A″ · D returns in octaves
sections.mNote: Both hands now strike the repeated note in octaves

sections.label: Coda · A glissando and two Ds
sections.mNote: A last climb reaches both ends of the keyboard

cues.title: One note, two hands
cues.text: The hands take turns striking D, the left an octave below the right. Semiquavers keep coming. Soon the left hand moves up and down in semitones while the right outlines a D-minor chord: a tune grows out of the repeated taps.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, Op. 11, opening. The written sequence of repeated Ds, chromatic left-hand patterns and D-minor triad is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Myaskovsky cannot keep quiet
cues.text: On 24 April 1912, Nikolay Myaskovsky writes to the critic Vladimir Derzhanovsky about the new Toccata. After praising its simple themes, he admits: “I can’t help but scream in delight.”
cues.evidence: Myaskovsky to Derzhanovsky, 11/24 April 1912, quoted in Simon Morrison’s Henle HN 1581 preface (2023), pp. IV–V, from Iosif Kunin’s collection of Myaskovsky documents (1981), p. 43. https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: The repeated note returns
cues.text: After the chromatic lines have spread across the keyboard, the opening repeated-note figure comes back. Prokofiev stretches its rhythm and briefly breaks the flow. The hands are about to move away from one another again.
cues.evidence: The Toccata’s first return of the repeated-note theme is followed by rhythmic augmentation, a short pause and independently descending triad figures. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quiet lion in Brooklyn
cues.text: At the Brooklyn Museum on 29 October 1918, Prokofiev plays before a reception for Boris Anisfeld’s paintings and theatre designs. He softens the Toccata for the guests, even leaving out notes. The next day’s reviewer describes a lion roaring as gently as a dove.
cues.evidence: Simon Morrison, Henle HN 1581 preface, p. V, citing the unsigned Brooklyn Daily Eagle review, 30 October 1918, p. 7. The image of lion and dove is paraphrased. https://www.henle.de/media/7f/27/66/1708068498/1581.pdf

cues.title: D fills both hands
cues.text: The opening D returns in alternating octaves, now played by both hands. The music has travelled through chromatic scales and colliding chords to reach the same note again. This time it fills much more of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, final return of the repeated-note theme; alternating D octaves in both hands. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two ends of the keyboard
cues.text: After slowing and stopping, the piano makes one last chromatic climb. An upward glissando sweeps into the ending: two D octaves, marked sforzando, at opposite ends of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, closing passage: slowdown, pause, chromatic ascent, glissando and final sforzando D octaves. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The opening figure comes back
transitions.from: A · One D between two hands
transitions.to: A′ · The repeated note returns quietly
transitions.how: The chromatic thirds lead back to the repeated-note figure. The pianist pares the writing down, then stretches the rhythm and pauses before the next passage. When both hands take up triad figures, they descend at different times, pulling apart the pattern they had shared.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, first return of the repeated-note theme and following triad passage. The score’s sequence is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev).

transitions.title: Chromatic lines arrive on D
transitions.how: Minor triads climb in the right hand while chromatic octaves descend in the left. The descending-thirds tune returns around D, then both hands take up repeated D octaves. The opening’s single notes have become a much larger two-handed attack.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata: contrary-motion chromatic writing, descending-thirds theme in D and the return of repeated D octaves. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)

transitions.title: A pause before the final climb
transitions.to: Coda · A glissando and two Ds
transitions.how: The repeated octaves slow and stop. The returning notes turn into a rising chromatic scale; octave chords and an upward glissando follow. Prokofiev finishes with two accented D octaves, one at each end of the keyboard.
transitions.evidence: Prokofiev, Toccata, final passage: slowdown and pause, chromatic ascent, glissando and two sforzando D octaves. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toccata_(Prokofiev)

composer.born: 27 April (15 April Old Style) 1891; Prokofiev himself gave 23 April, Sontsovka, Ukraine, then Russian Empire
composer.epithet: He gave Romeo and Juliet its singing strings and the piano some of the twentieth century’s sharpest teeth.
facts: Glière at Sontsovka, 1902–03; St Petersburg Conservatory, 1904–14
Russia · United States · Bavaria · Paris; settled in Moscow in 1936
The Love for Three Oranges · Romeo and Juliet · Cinderella · War and Peace
Seven symphonies, five piano concertos and nine completed piano sonatas

quote.text: It seemed to me that if Haydn had lived into our own time, he would have kept his way of writing while taking in something new.
quote.source: Prokofiev, short Autobiography (1941), recalling the summer of 1917; our translation

composer.background:
At Sontsovka, the Ukrainian estate his father managed, Prokofiev grew up hearing his mother play Beethoven and Chopin. She wrote down his first piano pieces; the earliest, an Indian Galop, dates from 1896. A trip to the Moscow opera in 1900 gave the eight-year-old an ambition of his own: The Giant, an opera for the family to perform at home. His mother eventually stopped playing when she saw that he had overtaken her. Sergei Taneyev recommended proper lessons, and Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka, teaching the boy who was already filling manuscript books.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen, bringing four operas, two sonatas, a symphony and piano pieces to the entrance examination. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Lyadov harmony and counterpoint; later Anna Esipova took charge of his piano playing. Nikolai Tcherepnin taught conducting and encouraged his taste for Haydn and Mozart. His fellow student Nikolai Myaskovsky became the friend to whom he sent scores and complaints for the rest of his life. In December 1908 Prokofiev played some of his first distinctive pieces, Suggestion diabolique among them, at St Petersburg’s Evenings of Contemporary Music. The following spring his examination pieces shocked Lyadov, who heard Scriabin in them. In the final piano competition of 1914, with Esipova ill, Prokofiev played his own First Concerto. Glazunov opposed him, but the Rubinstein Prize went to Prokofiev anyway: a grand piano.
